h1: Astringency in beer and why it can feel like stewed tea
title: Astringency in Beer Explained | Craft Beer School
desc: What astringency in beer is, why it feels like over-brewed tea and the brewing habits that cause it, from hot sparging to heavy dry hopping.
teaser: That dry, puckering grip on your gums is not bitterness. It is astringency. It usually starts at the mash tun.
standfirst: Astringency is the drying, rough feeling you get from tea left too long in the pot. In beer it is often mistaken for bitterness. This guide explains what causes it and how homebrewers can avoid it.
sections:
Astringency is a sensation, not a taste. It is the dry, rough, puckering feeling on your gums, cheeks and tongue, as if your mouth has been wiped with a cloth. Stewed tea, unripe banana and some red wines produce it. It is part of what our guide to mouthfeel and body calls texture.

It comes mostly from polyphenols, often called tannins. These compounds bind to proteins in your saliva and make them clump, so your mouth loses its slippery coating. That is why the dryness builds with each sip.

Many homebrewers taste astringency and call it bitterness. They are easy to confuse because they often turn up together. A simple test: bitterness is a taste, sensed mainly towards the back of the tongue. It can be clean. Astringency is a texture, felt across the whole mouth. It lingers as dryness after you swallow.

Some bitterness is welcome in almost every beer. Strong astringency usually is not, although a light touch can add structure to a dry stout or a hoppy ale. Our guide to bitterness perception explores the taste side.
Where it comes from: the grain husk

Barley husks are rich in polyphenols. Under normal conditions very little of them dissolves in the wort. Three things change that:

  • Hot sparging. Rinsing the grain with water much above about 76 to 78 °C dissolves more tannin from the husks.
  • Rising pH. As you sparge, the wort gets thinner and its pH climbs. Once the grain bed rises towards pH 6 and beyond, tannins come out much more easily. This is especially common with alkaline borewell water.
  • Over-sparging. Collecting the last weak runnings, below about 1.008 to 1.010, pulls the most tannin for the least sugar.

Our guide to lautering and sparging explains the process in more detail. The short version: sparge at about 75 to 77 °C, keep an eye on runnings gravity and stop collecting before the wort gets watery.

The husk is the main suspect, but not the only one.

  • Milling too fine. Shredding the husks increases their surface area, so more tannin leaks out. Aim for a crush that cracks the grain but leaves husks mostly whole, unless you use brew in a bag, where a finer crush is normal.
  • Heavy dry hopping. Hops contain polyphenols too. A beer dry hopped at very high rates can feel rough and grassy, sometimes with a burning sensation in the throat.
  • Spices and fruit skins. Long steeping of orange pith, grape or berry skins and some spices adds tannin.
  • Dark grains. Roasted barley and black malts can add dryness, which is part of a stout's character but harsh if overdone.

Change one thing at a time so you know what worked. A practical checklist:

  1. Check your sparge water temperature with a thermometer, not the dial on the heater.
  2. Measure the mash pH. Aim for 5.2 to 5.6. If your water is alkaline, add a small amount of lactic acid or use some RO water.
  3. Measure the gravity of your last runnings and stop above about 1.010.
  4. Inspect your crush. If the husks look like powder, open the mill gap.
  5. Shorten dry hop contact time, or use a little less hop and add it cold.

Many homebrewers find that a single change, usually sparge temperature or pH, solves most of it.
Can you rescue an astringent beer?

Partly. Polyphenols bind to proteins and drop out with time and cold, so a few weeks of cold conditioning can soften the edge. Finings such as gelatin or PVPP remove some polyphenols too. Blending with a smoother batch also helps.

But prevention works far better than cure. An astringent beer is usually a sign of a process habit that will repeat until you change it.
Training your mouth to notice it

A cheap way to learn the sensation: brew a cup of black tea for two minutes and another for ten minutes. Taste them side by side. The difference you feel on your gums is astringency. Then taste your own beer with that feeling in mind.

Telling astringency from bitterness and both from carbonation bite is a skill that improves with guided practice and reference samples.
faqs: Is astringency the same as bitterness?
No. Bitterness is a taste on the tongue. Astringency is a dry, rough feeling across the mouth caused by polyphenols binding to proteins in saliva.
What temperature should I sparge at to avoid astringency?
Keep the grain bed below about 76 to 78 °C. Most brewers sparge at around 75 to 77 °C.
Yes. Very heavy dry hopping or long contact times can add polyphenols and a rough, grassy dryness.
Some of it can soften with cold conditioning or finings, but prevention in the brewhouse is far more reliable.
